articles.title: Musk's Billion-Dollar Republican Election Play
articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoUS President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on October 8 [Evan Vucci/Reuters]By Reuters and The Associated Press12 Oct 2026Elon Musk, the trillionaire tech mogul and backer of far-right causes, has reportedly spent $366m since last year to buoy the Republican Party in the United States midterm elections. The New York Times first reported on Monday that Musk has spent $276m since July alone, including $158m for a super PAC focused on Republican Senate candidates, making him the largest single donor this year. Musk is considered a close ally of President Donald Trump, the leader of the Republican Party, and was a special government adviser to the White House last year. Musk’s political action committee, America PAC, has confirmed the spending totals. In a statement to The New York Times, a spokesperson framed the record amount as necessary to defend Congress from a Democratic takeover during the midterm races. “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo told the Times. The barrage of spending by Musk comes as Republican candidates are fighting to overcome Trump’s low popularity and rising concerns about the cost of living among US voters. Democrats are hoping to capitalise on voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s tenure to seize control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The influence of wealthy donors and PACs has long been the subject of criticism. Opponents argue that such spending distorts US politics in favour of powerful interests. Musk became the world’s first trillionaire in June, when his aerospace company SpaceX made its initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq stock exchange. The tech entrepreneur had previously said that he planned to step back from his involvement in US politics, stating in May that he had “done enough” and did not have plans for large spending efforts. Still, Musk has leveraged his tech holdings and wealth to support right-wing groups around the world. Last year, for instance, politicians in Germany accused Musk of trying to meddle in the national election. Musk has been a vocal backer of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been accused of adopting a discriminatory stance on immigration and other issues. Voters in the US will head to the polls on November 3 to cast their ballots in the midterms, which will decide key state and local races, as well as congressional majorities. The Republican Party is considered to have a sizeable financial advantage over the Democrats ahead of the race, with heavy spending from groups such as MAGA Inc, a pro-Trump super PAC named for the president’s “Make America Great Again” movement. As of August, MAGA Inc reportedly had $416m in its coffers. The tracking site AdImpact found that it had spent $22m over the past month alone on the tight race unfolding for the open Senate seat in Texas. Trump has also increased his campaign activities, hosting a string of rallies in the final weeks before the election to help Republicans push their message. But Democrats appear confident that the Republicans’ spending advantage will not be enough to counter the effects of growing dissatisfaction with Trump. “Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

articles.title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs Warn AI Chip Capital Crunch
articles.content: LivestreamMenuIntel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom."[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.In this article SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models. "[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns. "If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said. Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity. The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns. Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands. "[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now." He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online. Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure. "There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030. Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power. But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said. Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau. Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

PHOTO: AFP Published Oct 13, 2026, 08:06 AM Updated Oct 13, 2026, 09:07 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise The New York Times, AFP and The Economist joined the SPUR coalition to stop AI firms using publisher content without permission. SPUR now has more than 80 members in over 20 countries and is building standards to track AI use and support licensing deals. Publishers are also suing AI firms and losing traffic as AI search answers reduce clicks, with Google referrals down 33% globally, Reuters Institute said. AI generated NEW YORK- The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Oct 12 joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing artificial intelligence firms from using or profiting from their content without permission. The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil’s National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press. Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier in October , USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement. OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organisations, including the New York Times. SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website. “Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist,” Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times’ head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement. Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat. SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardise how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work. articles.title: French Supermarkets Hit by Refrigerator Cyberattack
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Around 150 Intermarche supermarket stores were hit by cyberattacks on the night of Oct 11. PHOTO: EPA Published Oct 13, 2026, 07:25 AM Updated Oct 13, 2026, 09:11 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Hackers attacked hundreds of French supermarkets on Oct 11 and disabled fridges, forcing stores to throw away meat, frozen food and vegetables. About 150 Intermarche stores, fewer than 100 Cooperative U stores and 80 Carrefour sites were hit. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France” and is helping customers. The attacks raised fears of physical sabotage through “operational technology” systems. Experts said older Danfoss equipment lacked updates, and France is preparing to protect critical infrastructure. AI generated PARIS - Hundreds of supermarkets in France were hit by cyberattacks on the night of Oct 11 that disabled refrigeration systems and forced stores to throw out damaged food, following warnings that hackers are seeking to cause physical damage. Around 150 Intermarche stores were hit, a spokesman for owner Groupement Mousquetaires told Bloomberg. Hackers accessed cooling systems and set them to defrost, with refrigerators and freezers heating to 50 deg C for around six hours. Meat, frozen items and vegetables had to be tossed out. Mousquetaires said the systems were managed by Danish refrigeration firm Danfoss and that it would be up to the supplier to file a complaint with the authorities. Cooperative U was also hit by the cyberattacks, chief executive Dominique Schelcher said on X. Fewer than a hundred of its stores were affected, Agence France-Presse reported. A spokesperson for Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were impacted out of a total of 6,000 sites. Some Leclerc stores were also targeted, BFM said. Leclerc did not immediately respond to a Bloomberg request for comment. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France” and working with customers to implement mitigation measures. It was not immediately clear who was behind the refrigeration cyberattacks, but the intrusions occurred against a backdrop of disruptive cyberattacks internationally. In August, Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that hackers were increasingly seeking to cause physical disruption with their attacks, which it linked in part to increased geopolitical instability. The centre said that such attacks were targeting multiple sectors globally and had been carried out by a range of threat actors. Hackers are more frequently associated with stealing data and extorting companies. But they can also target what are known as operational technology systems, which control physical processes and equipment, such as machinery or temperature controls in refrigeration systems. In the US in July, suspected Iranian hackers targeted water facilities in at least seven states and in some cases degraded water operations. Unidentified hackers separately targeted oil and gas tankers this summer, temporarily accessing the propulsion system of a tanker approaching the Texas coast. In September, French president Emmanuel Macron said that he had instructed his government to prepare a plan to protect France’s critical infrastructure and defence industrial and technological base against drone and cyberattacks. He said the country was facing intensifying hostile actions from Russia . Muhammad Yahya Patel, virtual chief information security officer and cybersecurity adviser for EMEA at the cybersecurity firm Huntress, said the refrigeration attacks are the type that the security industry has been warning about as the “next frontier for sabotage attacks. “They’ve now been weaponised against food retail infrastructure in one of Europe’s largest economies. The immediate financial consequences are significant and visible.” Danfoss spokesperson Lars Grubak Lohff told Bloomberg that the majority of the affected products are old technologies, including the company’s AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 refrigeration systems, which no longer receive software or security updates. “Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions,” Lohff wrote. In August, cybersecurity researchers at Team82, part of Claroty, wrote a report flagging vulnerabilities in Danfoss controllers used to manage refrigeration in supermarkets and other cold storage facilities. The group said it had found a hidden authentication mechanism that could be used to tamper with the operations of refrigeration systems. Danfoss sold a €500 million (S$714 million) 5.5-year bond on Oct 12 that drew more than €3 billion of investor bids, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. The lead managers moved the pricing level by as much as 37 basis points tighter during the process. BLOOMBERG France Hacking Food security

articles.title: HK Police Launch AI National Security Platform for Schools
articles.content: Hong Kong police have launched an artificial intelligence-powered national security education platform for pupils. Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026. Photo: HKPF, via Facebook. The NSmarties AI Interactive Platform was officially launched last week at a ceremony at Precious Blood Primary School in Ap Lei Chau, with about 700 pupils attending, police said in a social media post . Police commissioner Joe Chow said during the ceremony that the campaign aimed to “plant the seeds of national security in students’ hearts,” according to the post. See also: Hong Kong schools on ‘frontline’ of preventing ‘soft resistance,’ education minister says The platform, jointly developed by police and Hong Kong Qianfan Technology, allows students to generate personalised stories centred on China’s “holistic approach to national security” – a framework advocated by President Xi Jinping that covers areas ranging from politics and the economy to ecology and technology. It also features the voices of Chow and security chief Chris Tang, who explain the city’s national security laws and security information. Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026. Photo: HKPF, via Facebook. The ceremony marked a “milestone” for national security entering the city’s schools using innovative technologies, police said. The NSmarties platform was first unveiled on National Security Education Day in April, but it was not fully launched to the public at that time. Hong Kong has strengthened national security education alongside a crackdown since Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 following the 2019 protests and unrest. Beijing inserted national security legislation directly into Hong Kong’s mini-constitution in June 2020 following a year of pro-democracy protests and unrest. It criminalised subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts – broadly defined to include disruption to transport and other infrastructure. The move gave police sweeping new powers and led to hundreds of arrests amid new legal precedents , while dozens of civil society groups disappeared . The authorities say it restored stability and peace to the city, rejecting criticism from trade partners , the UN and NGOs . articles.title: AI Company Offers Police Tool for House Identification
articles.content: • AI Company Lets Cops Pinpoint Specific Houses Based on a Single Interior Photo · Oct 12, 2026 at 9:00 AM Raven, previously called GeoSpy, lets cops figure out what specific Airbnb or Zillow property a photo was taken in. An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb.  The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy . Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes. In a post on LinkedIn earlier this month , Graylark CEO Daniel Heinen wrote the company was introducing “the ability to geolocate interior images across millions of short-term rental units worldwide.” An accompanying demo video shows someone taking a photo from X of a washer/dryer unit inside a building. They upload it to Raven, select “Find Property: Interior and exterior property geolocation,” and then choose a region to search. 💡 Do you know anything else about this technology or others like it? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. After a couple of seconds, the map interface zooms in on an area in Charlotte, North Carolina. On the right hand side, the screen displays a list of results. The top one reads, “Renovated! Walk Uptown/located in 2 Hot Spots!” That result directly quotes the language on a specific Airbnb listing in Charlotte, and the photos in the Airbnb listing show the same property. Later in the video, the Raven user takes a photo of a bathroom from social media. They upload it to Raven, and the tool points to an area of Montecito, California. The top result says, “Montecito Miramar Beach House on the Sand.” 404 Media found that result directly quotes a listing on the short term rental site Vrbo. In other words, from a single photo, Raven appears to be able to quickly find the specific home it was taken in, without using location data or other metadata attached to the image. In the demonstrations the videos were from social media, but in practice they could be from anywhere a law enforcement officer has obtained them. This is also not a reverse image search: a reverse image search would take an image then find an identical one posted somewhere else on the internet. What Raven is doing, instead, is identifying unique characteristics in the photo, then finding what are likely other photos from the same property on sites like Airbnb, even if those photos are not exactly the same, or even if time has passed between them being taken. In another post , Heinen wrote, “For investigators working trafficking and exploitation cases, that connection can turn an unidentified room into a location lead they can verify and pursue.” Raven is not limited to short term rentals, according to other demo videos. In a third example posted last year, Raven traces a photo of an interior room to a specific address in San Francisco. The interface returns other interior photos of the property; 404 Media found these are exactly the same photos as those posted on Zillow, indicating that Raven is at least pulling data from Zillow in some form.  Another video posted last week shows Raven identifying a particular hotel, too. A screenshot from a Raven promotional video on LinkedIn. In another video, a part of the interface says, “City-specific property AI to determine an address.” That phrase implies the property search isn’t necessarily worldwide, but dependent on an AI model built specifically for that city. When 404 Media reported earlier this year that at least two law enforcement agencies have bought access to Raven, emails showed the MDSO had access to a custom model specifically trained for Miami-Dade County. “In 2026, we’re investing heavily in interior geolocation across U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments,” Heinen adds in the post. Graylark trained Raven on millions of images from around the world. When the tool first launched, it was focused on identifying distinct geographical markers like architecture and soil. Now Raven extends that same idea into buildings.  In an interview with the tech publication Indicator last year, Heinen discussed some of how the building interior searching capability came to be. “I’ll be honest, we didn't train it to do that,” he said. “That was kind of an ‘Oh shit’ moment for us. GeoSpy 1.0 couldn't do that. As we trained GeoSpy 2.0, we were just kind of red teaming and testing it out and I think I had a picture of my girlfriend just taking a selfie in the bathroom. I was curious what it would say and I dropped it in there and it put a pin on San Francisco. I was like, ‘Well hold on, wait a minute. That doesn't make any sense. It’s just a picture in a bathroom.’ And then I went over to Zillow and I just started screenshotting images and nine out of 10 of them it would get the right city.” “We have huge datasets that we train the models on and these are geotagged images from all over. Usually, we would assume that the images are all outdoor images. I'm assuming some of those images would probably have some indoors, whether it's people at a party or just taking pictures of food on their counter. The models must have learned some details that relate to different locations,” he continued. Airbnb told 404 Media in email “Protecting our community's privacy is important to us — that’s why location metadata is excluded from listing photos, hosts are given the option to show only an approximate location of their listing, and a home’s address is shared with a guest only after a reservation is confirmed. We also have technical safeguards in place to try to limit automated data collection from our site.” Airbnb stressed it has no relationship with Graylark, that its terms of service prohibit scraping, and that the company is reviewing this case. Zillow told 404 Media that scraping data is against its terms of use, and when necessary it pursues legal avenues. Vrbo did not respond to multiple requests for comment. It is unclear if the examples shown in the marketing videos are truly representative of Raven’s speed or capabilities. While law enforcement agencies have paid for access to Raven, it hasn’t always impressed. Joseph R. Peguero Rivera, from MDSO’s Public Affairs Office, previously told 404 Media “To date, use of GeoSpy has been limited and largely exploratory. While it has been reviewed in a small number of cases, it has not resulted in any significant investigative breakthroughs or arrests. No case outcomes were driven solely or primarily by information generated by the tool.”  404 Media first covered Raven in January 2025. At the time, the tool was available to essentially anyone, and some people in the company’s Discord server asked for help stalking women. A day after 404 Media contacted Graylark for comment, the company restricted access to the tool to only government agencies and enterprise users. In a September X post , Heinen said Alexandr Wang, now head of AI at Meta, was an angel investor in Graylark. Wang did not respond to a request for comment. In a LinkedIn post earlier this year, Heinen showed Raven being used against a video of people vandalizing a Flock camera. Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more. articles.title: European Productivity Lag: Beyond US and China
articles.content: Darren Staples/Getty Images Europe Must Look Beyond the US and China to Solve Its Productivity Problem Oct 12, 2026 Dani Rodrik Given America and China’s lead in AI and other cutting-edge innovations, it is not surprising that much of the European economic policy debate revolves around the need to emulate and catch up with these two technological superpowers. In fact, neither the US nor China offers a relevant or attractive model for Europe. CAMBRIDGE—Europe faces a productivity crisis. Over the past quarter-century, its labor productivity has risen only half as rapidly as that of the United States, widening the gap between American and European incomes. Thanks to higher public expenditures, stronger labor-market institutions, and superior safety nets, the benefits of European economic growth are better distributed. articles.content: Any Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Any Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (known as PHEVs) imported above the new quota level will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3% Business live – latest updates VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed. Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week . The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures. Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces Read more Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will. China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU. Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing. “We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said. Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement. On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China. Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China. Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports. “We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official. Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU. “I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said. articles.title: IonQ Acquires Cybersecurity Firm Elisity for $1.3B
articles.content: IonQ announced Monday that it will acquire Elisity, a zero-trust network security firm, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion that folds enterprise access control into the quantum computing company’s expanding cybersecurity business. Elisity, founded in 2019, sells a software policy layer that governs which users, devices, workloads and AI agents can communicate across a network, independent of the underlying network technology. The California-based company reports more than 100 global deployments and says revenue and customer counts have doubled year over year, with no churn among deployed customers. Maryland-based IonQ, whose core business is quantum computing, has been building a security arm around post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution, technologies intended to replace or supplement encryption that future quantum computers may be able to break.  The combination addresses what the companies describe as a two-front problem: conventional attacks that operate at machine speed, and the risk that encrypted data could be retained until quantum decryption becomes practical, a concept known as “harvest now, decrypt later.” “Our customers need to contain attacks today, put AI to work safely, and prepare for quantum risk,” Elisity CEO James Winebrenner wrote in a blog post announcing the deal.  IonQ Chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi struck a more urgent note in a release announcing the deal: “Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted,” he said, referencing the point at which quantum computers could break current encryption technology.  Both governments and the technology industry have accelerated their timelines to adopt post-quantum cryptography over the past few years. This is partly due to a belief among executives in the U.S. quantum sector that Chinese scientists and labs have achieved breakthroughs across several different fields of quantum computing over the past two years. The Trump administration recently issued an executive order directing federal agencies to boost the domestic quantum industry and move up internal timelines for migrating to PQC encryption from 2035 to 2030. Google, a potential industry bellwether, and other companies have opted to move their own migration timelines to 2029. Winebrenner told CyberScoop those deadlines are easier to set than to meet. Enterprises will hace to start with identifying the information and operations that need protecting, then mapping the identities, communications and cryptographic dependencies that support them. “You won’t replace every legacy system at once,” he said. The approach is to migrate what can be migrated, test interoperability and operational impact, and tightly control access around systems that need more time. Segmentation helps contain threats, he added, but does not replace the cryptographic upgrades. Elisity’s planned role in that transition is to connect identity data to cryptographic decision-making. Its roadmap would extend its IdentityGraph product with cryptographic inventory and risk information, allowing customers to rank post-quantum upgrades by business risk. The deal also reflects how AI agents are reshaping network security. Elisity’s platform already treats AI agents and other non-human identities as subjects of access policy, and the company has joined the Open Secure AI Alliance with priorities that include least-privilege rules for sanctioned agents, containment of agentic threats and control of unsanctioned AI. Winebrenner identified the hardest unresolved problem in agent control as maintaining trustworthy identity and authorization as an agent’s task, tools and delegated permissions change. “Knowing an agent is approved is only the beginning,” he said. “You need to understand whose authority it is exercising, what it needs to reach right now and when that access should end.” His prescription is least privilege down to the task: “An AI agent should have access only to the resources its task requires, including when it interacts with older infrastructure.” The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval. articles.title: World Bank Warns of AI 'Tsunami' in Job Market
articles.content: LivestreamMenuIMF’s Georgieva warned AI is hitting labor markets like a “slow-moving tsunami,” with about 40% of jobs worldwide eventually affected and young graduates most exposed.Singapore President Tharman urged governments to make "crisis-era" support measures permanent and incentivize firms to hire young graduates.World Bank’s Banga backed “small AI” tools and called on governments to unlock private capital to create jobs for 1.2 billion young people. Kristalina Georgieva (R), managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), shakes hands with Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam at the IMF Annual Meetings Curtain Raiser in Singapore on October 7, 2026. Roslan Rahman | Afp | Getty ImagesBANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

The Marcos administration details its initiatives aimed to be completed by 2028 under the second National Cybersecurity Plan AT A GLANCE The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s administration developed the second iteration of the National Cybersecurity Plan (NCSP) to enhance national cybersecurity by 2028. The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration developed the second iteration of the National Cybersecurity Plan (NCSP) . This plan aims to address the country’s growing vulnerability to cyber threats and achieve the following outcomes by the end of Marcos’ term in 2028: Proactive protection and security of national cyberspace Increased workforce capability Strengthened policy framework According to the DICT, the plan aligns with the country’s Development Plan , National Security Strategy, National Cybercrime Strategy, and other cybersecurity strategies by national government agencies. On April 6, 2024, Marcos officially gave the green light to carry out the plan and adopted it through Executive Order No. 58 .  Below are the government efforts listed under the NCSP. 1. National Fiber Backbone (NFB) : A high-speed, government-owned nationwide broadband network. This allows the recalibration of Government Network (GovNet) infrastructure security and unites all national and local government agencies into one Wide Area Network (WAN). The initiative began rolling out its initial phase in 2023 and launched Phase 1 of the Mindanao Integrated Government Network last June. 2. National government cloud platform : It will be used for storing confidential government data in close coordination with the Department of National Defense (DND), Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), and Philippine National Police (PNP) to secure the physical internetwork of GovNet and the NFB. It also includes the landing stations and submarine cable systems. The DICT kickstarted its Cloud First Policy in 2017 and has built on it ever since. In 2024, the e-GovCloud initiative hosted 1,277 government systems . 3. Strengthened National Computer Emergency Response Team (NCERT) and Modernized National Security Operations Center (NSOC): On April 7, 60 more agencies were onboarded as part of the national plan. This expands the operation’s coverage nationwide. These teams would handle incident response, investigation, government Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) services, threat monitoring and hunting, malware analysis, and threat advisories. A centralized system accessible by other agencies would also be in place to delegate incident tickets for monitoring. 4. National cybersecurity threat database : An accessible database that categorizes threats and is uploadable to cybersecurity defense systems. In 2024, the DICT said NSOC monitors over two million cyber threats per day . However, as of writing, the database is not yet publicly accessible. 5. Partnerships with Public Telecommunication Entities (PTEs) and Internet Service Providers (ISPs) : The DICT, National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), and telecom providers would establish reporting protocols to assist in security countermeasures to detect threats and malicious activities early and combat malware outbreaks. Major telecommunications companies, such as Globe Telecom, Smart Communications, PLDT, Converge ICT Solutions Incorporated, Infinivan, and PT&T, have begun their partnership with the DICT in 2025. This laid the groundwork for the nationwide rollout of the Protective Domain Name System (PDNS), which scans DNS queries in real time and blocks access to dangerous websites, including those used for phishing, malware, and the spread of fake news. 6. Misinformation combat : On April 14, the DICT partnered with the Presidential Communications Office and the Department of Justice to launch “ Oplan Kontra Fake News ,” an inter-agency framework designed to curb the spread of disinformation and AI-generated deepfakes. 7. National Cybersecurity Intelligence Fusion Center: The plan looks to establish a nationwide network of CERTs with clearly defined roles and a new incident response model. The NCSP detailed a new workflow and hierarchical model, with the DICT NCERT and the Defense CERT as top command. As of July, the DICT partnered with the Korea International Cooperation Agency to build a physical cybersecurity center in Valenzuela.  8. Securing submarine cable infrastructure: The DICT will coordinate with government agencies such as the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to develop a map of all cables and them to prevent damage due to theft, anchorage, earthquakes, and major climate disturbances. Earlier this year, the DICT partnered with Australia’s Cable Connectivity and Resilience Centre to develop a framework to protect the country’s subsea cables and submitted the analysis to Marcos. Telco companies PLDT, Globe, and Converge also joined the agency to plan a cable system that will loop around the country , which may be completed in 24 months. 9. Bilateral and multilateral international cooperation : The plan looks to expand existing agreements with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the United Nations, Interpol, and other bilateral agreements with other countries. The country has partnered with Korea to build a cybersecurity center. It also had a Cyber-Digital Policy dialogue with the United States in 2024 to strengthen both countries’ ICT, their resilience to cybersecurity threats, and the growth of the digital economy. 1. October as Cybersecurity Awareness Month : On October 2, 2023, Marcos signed Proclamation No. 353 , changing the commemoration of Cybersecurity Awareness Month from September to October. This coincides with the international cybersecurity month celebrations. 2. ICT Academy : The ICT Literacy and Competency Development Bureau (ILCDB) was upgraded to ICT Academy on October 1 to develop a highly skilled workforce capable of addressing cybersecurity challenges. It would also engage with research initiatives and collaborate with industry partners, government agencies, and international bodies to ensure a globally accepted approach. 3. Cybersecurity jobs in government: The DICT would collaborate with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and the Civil Service Commission (CSC) to create official job titles, hiring qualifications, and specialized exams for cybersecurity career service positions in the government. Under the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of Republic Act No. 12254 , signed on March 24, the three agencies were required to develop guidelines establishing specialized cybersecurity positions across all national agencies, including local governments, state universities and colleges (SUCs), and government-owned or controlled corporations. 4. Partnerships with local and international training providers : The department would work with private industry leaders to create online short courses that would be internationally recognized and certified. It has already secured a multi-year deal with Google to enhance the country’s cybersecurity defense. The partnership would train public servants to use Gemini Enterprise and Google Workspace, with the end goal of training 200,000 people nationwide over the next 18 months. 5. Cybersecurity programs and scholarships : The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and SUCs are encouraged to develop cybersecurity degree programs. The DICT would also partner with TESDA in creating National Certification in various cybersecurity skills. These programs would also be included in partial and full scholarships. In 2019, CHED has already listed cybersecurity as one of the priority courses for scholarship programs under Memorandum Order No. 5, s. 2019 . As of writing, some universities offer cybersecurity programs, including Mapúa University , De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde , and Lyceum of the Philippines University . 6. National and international hacking competitions: The DICT would organize regional and national hacking competitions where winners would take part in international competitions. The agency would also build a network of experts, resource persons, and trainers. The DICT kicked off HackForGov in 2019, an annual nationwide cybersecurity competition. It has become an annual competition since then, with different regions hosting the event. Winners would eventually represent the country in the annual Cyber SEA Game . 1. Strengthening National Cybersecurity Inter-Agency Committee : Marcos has reinforced the established committee, created under E.O. 189, s. 2015 . The committee would serve as a convergence hub of different government agencies and the main forum for information sharing, planning, and ensuring policies don’t conflict with other interests. The President has then mandated the DICT to submit biannual implementation reports on national cyber policies. 2. Executive Order on Critical Infrastructure and Critical Information Infrastructure: E.O. 119, s. 2026 updated government data classification, and the framework for data security. This covers all digital or hybrid government-owned data, including private service providers that handle government data. 3. Mandatory security labelling of devices: The plan looks to require routers and switches sold in the market to be labeled to inform the public about the security of the products. 4. Revision on VAPT service providers’ accreditation: The DICT revised the existing accreditation of VAPT service providers last January under Department Circular No. HRA-001, s. 2026 . The revisions would add customer feedback through complaint mechanisms and train service providers on managing them. 5. Establish policies, guidelines, and procedures on network security systems: The DICT would partner with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), Department of Science and Technology, the academe, and industry partners to develop network security system protocols. The agency has already released Department Circular No. 003, s. 2024 , mandating all government agencies to adhere to security measures and response protocols. This also includes rerouting internet traffic to DICT-managed PDNS, automated vulnerability scans, and sharing information with the NSOC. 6. Minimum cybersecurity standards : Under Republic Act NO. 12254 , the DICT was prescribed to implement minimum information security standards for government systems. In March 2026, an IRR was issued requiring all government agencies to comply. 7. Legislative Agenda and Enactments: The DICT would endorse key legislative measures to Congress to resolve economic challenges, information asymmetry, and establish legal cybersecurity protections. In 2026, the House of Representatives approved on third and final reading House Bill No. 9605 , or the proposed “National Cybersecurity and Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Act of 2026.” The bill is aligned with the administration’s Digital Transformation Framework and seeks to establish mandatory cybersecurity standards and certification systems, ensuring consistent defense protocols for public and private sectors. – Rappler.com Add to Preferred Sources Share in Chat Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Related Topics DICT Ferdinand Marcos Jr. information technology and computer science internet in the Philippines {{ item.sitename }} {{ item.primarytopic }} {{ item.primarytopic }} {{ item.title }}

articles.title: World's First Interactive Satellite-to-Smartphone Map
articles.content: Business Wire via ITWeb, BOSTON, 12 Oct 2026 Opensignal D2D Satellite Map Opensignal, a global independent consumer connectivity analytics and insights company, today launched the Opensignal D2D Satellite Map , the world’s first interactive, real-world depiction of where direct-to-device (D2D) satellite connections with smartphones are happening across the globe. Every point on the map, which will be updated monthly, represents a location where smartphones have connected to a D2D service since January 2026, extracted from Opensignal’s billions of real-world measurements. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261011884935/en/ “D2D is reshaping who can deliver mobile coverage, and where, because the phone in your pocket can now reach a satellite directly. Until now, the industry has had to make decisions without knowing where momentum and adoption are real,” said Mike Sandy, President, Market Performance at Opensignal. “The Opensignal D2D Satellite Map provides an independent view of where D2D is taking hold across the globe, so decisions about partnerships, spectrum and devices can be grounded in how consumers are actually connecting today. As D2D matures, that view will only become more important.” While satellite broadband is a well-established offering for home and business internet, D2D is a newer, rapidly growing area. Many of today’s standard smartphones can now connect directly to satellites, extending mobile coverage to places terrestrial networks don’t, or can’t, reach. As of August 2026, the Global mobile Suppliers Association (GSA) reports that 23 partnerships have launched satellite-to-cellphone services. Current D2D services are largely limited to text messaging, emergency alerts and a small set of apps, constrained by limited spectrum, early-generation satellite and handset hardware, and standards that are still evolving. Mobile operators and satellite companies are working toward enabling voice and higher-speed data, while regulators are weighing how to make more spectrum available for D2D. In addition to where connections are happening, Opensignal expects to show how well these connections perform as D2D services mature, similar to its mobile network experience analyses. You can find the Opensignal D2D Satellite Map at https://d2d.opensignal.com . Its insights are fueled by 50+ billion daily data points from over 100 million devices worldwide on mobile, fixed broadband, and satellite networks, alongside pricing, promotions, and competitive conditions, showing how consumers actually experience connectivity and why they switch. In addition to public network benchmark reports and market insights, Opensignal delivers this intelligence through its portfolio of premium solutions, including Opensignal Network Experience Suite, Opensignal Subscriber Analytics, Frontline Network Experience, and GeoResults. Headquartered in Boston, Opensignal has offices in Canada, the UK, Poland and Singapore. For more information, visit https://opensignal.com . articles.title: Government Warns Against Online Incitement
articles.content: By Staff Writer , ITWeb Johannesburg, 12 Oct 2026 Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration chairperson Mmamoloko Kubayi. Government has warned that individuals using social media to incite violence, intimidate foreign nationals or mobilise unlawful activities will face the consequences of their actions, as tensions surrounding migration and asylum applications continue. The Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Migration on Sunday raised concern about the circulation of inflammatory and misleading content on digital platforms, saying such material could provoke hostility against foreign nationals, public officials and State institutions. “Freedom of expression is protected by the Constitution; however, the incitement of violence, intimidation, hate speech and criminal conduct are not protected and will not be tolerated,” said IMC chairperson Mmamoloko Kubayi. The committee said law enforcement agencies were monitoring developments closely and would act against individuals or groups seeking to encourage, organise, facilitate or commit acts of violence and public disorder, whether online or offline. “Those who use digital platforms to incite criminal conduct should be reminded that such conduct may constitute a criminal offence and will be dealt with in accordance with the law,” Kubayi said. See also Digital platforms monitor risks amid protests in SA Home Affairs goes digital to catch ghosts The warning comes amid heightened public debate over migration and the implications of the Constitutional Court judgement on the processing of asylum applications, handed down on 7 July. The court declared sections of the Refugees Act, which allowed for immigration officials to deport an asylum seeker if they are in the country without a transit visa, unconstitutional. A transit visa is issued at a port of entry to allow a person to travel to a refugee reception centre and apply for asylum. The IMC acknowledged that discussions surrounding the judgement had generated uncertainty, speculation and heightened tensions in some communities. It called on members of the public, civil society organisations, community formations and political stakeholders to exercise restraint while the legal processes underway are resolved. The committee reiterated that South Africans have a constitutional right to assemble, demonstrate and present grievances peacefully. However, it stressed that this right did not extend to intimidation, looting, malicious damage to property, public violence or the obstruction of lawful activities. “South Africa remains a constitutional democracy governed by the rule of law. Matters relating to asylum, migration and border management must be addressed through lawful processes and not through misinformation, intimidation, incitement, or acts of violence,” Kubayi said. The IMC also acknowledged engagements with representatives of civil society organisations, including Operation Dudula, March and March, the United Civic Movement, the South African Council of Churches, South Africa First and the Alexander Fiela Movement. The representatives had presented their frustrations, feedback from their stakeholders and communities, as well as proposals on how government should address migration-related concerns. The committee said it welcomed engagements and feedback from South Africans as government worked to address the challenges arising from the Constitutional Court judgement. Share
